title: Choosing the best source for a purpose
blurb: Match each research need to the source that is most authoritative, most current and most specific for it.
question: A parent needs the correct dose of a children's allergy medicine for a 6-year-old. The choices are a parenting forum, a popular health video, the medicine's package insert and a general encyclopedia article on allergies. Which source is best, and why is the most popular one wrong?

teach.body: Formally, the best source for a task is the one that is most specific, most current and most authoritative for that particular need. In plain English: there is no single 'best source' for everything. A dictionary is perfect for a pronunciation and useless for bus times. Start with what you need to know, then ask who would know it most reliably and most recently.

items.label: Current
items.display: up to date for the need

teach.h: Four questions for any source task
items: What exactly do I need: a fact, a definition, an overview, instructions or someone's firsthand view?
Who is the authority on that: the manufacturer, a government agency, a dictionary, the person themselves?
How current must it be? Schedules, doses and health guidance change; a word's pronunciation rarely does.
Is it specific to my case: this drug, this city, this year, this school?

teach.h: Match the need to the source
Popular and new are not the same as best
teach.body: The most shared post, the most viewed video or the newest blog is not automatically the best source. A transit rider's video from last spring is popular but may be out of date and unofficial; the transit authority's current schedule is both current and authoritative. Likewise, a 2009 page on vaccine schedules may come from an expert but is too old for current guidance. Weigh all three: authority, currency, specificity.

teach.text: Wrong answers favor the most popular source, the most recent source regardless of who wrote it, or a source that is reliable but too general (a national yearly summary for a question about one county this month). Also, a .org address does not make a source unbiased: check who runs it.

teach.body: Hannah Nguyen, applying to a nursing program, needs three things: each school's current admission requirements, the meaning of 'prerequisite GPA', and how a nursing pioneer felt about her training. For requirements she uses each school's official admissions page (authoritative, current, specific), not a forum thread. For the term she checks the program's glossary. For the pioneer's feelings she reads the pioneer's own letters, not a modern summary.

items: The best source depends on the task: relevant, authoritative, current, specific.
Doses: package insert or prescriber information. Bus times: the transit authority's current schedule.
Pronunciation or meaning: a dictionary. A person's own view: their letters or diary.
Most popular or most recent does not mean most reliable.
A reliable but general source loses to an equally reliable, more specific one.

summary: You can now choose the best source for a specific research need by weighing relevance, authority, currency and specificity. You can also reject sources that are popular, recent or general but not the most reliable for the task.

A.q: Rachel needs to know how much of a children's liquid fever reducer to give her 4-year-old daughter. Which source should she use?
options: A parenting blog with thousands of daily readers
The dosing chart on the medicine's package label
A general encyclopedia article about fevers
A video posted by a parent with a large following
A.why: The package label gives official, product-specific dosing information from the manufacturer, which is exactly what Rachel needs.

whyNot.0: A popular blog is not an official dosing authority, and its advice may not match this product.
whyNot.2: An encyclopedia article on fevers is too general to give a dose for a specific product.
whyNot.3: A popular video is not an authoritative source for medicine doses.

A.q: Omar wants to know what time the Route 12 bus leaves the hospital stop next Saturday. Which source is most reliable?
options: A printed timetable he picked up two years ago
A rider forum where people post about late buses
The city transit authority's current online schedule
A coworker who rode Route 12 on a weekday last month
A.why: The transit authority's current schedule is both official and up to date, and it covers weekend times.

whyNot.0: A two-year-old timetable may be out of date.
whyNot.1: A forum reports riders' experiences, not the official schedule.
whyNot.3: A coworker's weekday trip does not show Saturday times and is not official.

A.q: A student is unsure how to pronounce 'hemoglobin' before giving a class presentation. Which source should she check?
options: An almanac
An atlas
A dictionary
A thesaurus
A.why: A dictionary gives pronunciation guides along with definitions.

whyNot.0: An almanac compiles yearly facts and statistics, not pronunciations.
whyNot.3: A thesaurus lists synonyms, usually without pronunciation guides.

B.q: A student is writing about how Clara Barton herself felt while caring for wounded soldiers during the Civil War. Which source would be most useful?
options: Letters Barton wrote to friends during the war
A 2015 textbook chapter on Civil War medicine
An encyclopedia entry summarizing Barton's life
A recent documentary on the American Red Cross
B.why: Barton's own letters from the time are firsthand records of her feelings, which is exactly what the student needs.

whyNot.1: A textbook interprets the period in general and may say little about Barton's own feelings.
whyNot.2: An encyclopedia gives a brief overview, not her personal reactions.
whyNot.3: A documentary on the Red Cross interprets later history and is secondhand.

B.q: A student needs the current recommended schedule for childhood vaccines. Which source is best?
options: A 2011 nursing textbook chapter on immunizations
A popular wellness influencer's video on vaccines
A neighbor whose children are all fully vaccinated
The current guidance page of a federal health agency
B.why: A federal health agency's current page is authoritative and up to date; vaccine schedules change, so currency matters.

whyNot.0: The textbook may be expert, but a 2011 schedule may be out of date.
whyNot.1: An influencer is not an authority on vaccine schedules, however popular.
whyNot.2: A neighbor's experience is personal, not official guidance.

B.q: A student wants a brief overview of the history of the stethoscope before reading more deeply. Which source is the best starting point?
options: A general encyclopedia entry on the stethoscope
A 2023 journal study testing digital stethoscopes
A hospital's purchase records for stethoscopes
A cardiologist's blog post on her favorite model
B.why: An encyclopedia compiles a brief, general overview of a topic, which suits background reading before deeper research.

whyNot.1: A single study of digital models is too narrow for a historical overview.
whyNot.2: Purchase records are raw data about one hospital, not a history.
whyNot.3: A personal blog post about a favorite model is an opinion, not a history.

C.q: A school nurse wants to know how many flu cases have been reported in her county this month. Which source is most useful?
options: A national flu summary covering last year's season
The county health department's latest weekly report
A news story about flu season trends across the US
A medical textbook chapter explaining how flu spreads
C.why: The county health department's latest weekly report is official, current and specific to her county and this month.

whyNot.0: A national summary from last year is neither local nor current.
whyNot.2: A national news story is not specific to her county and is secondhand.
whyNot.3: A textbook explains the disease but gives no current local case counts.

C.q: Kayla is comparing the prerequisite courses required by three nursing programs for next fall. Which source should she rely on most?
options: A discussion thread where applicants share tips
A magazine ranking of nursing schools from 2021
A friend who applied to one of the programs last year
Each program's official admissions page for next fall
C.why: Each program's own admissions page is authoritative, current for next fall and specific to that program's requirements.

whyNot.0: Applicants' tips are secondhand and may be outdated or wrong.
whyNot.1: A 2021 ranking is out of date and ranks schools rather than listing current prerequisites.
whyNot.2: A friend's experience covers one program and last year's rules.

C.q: A pharmacy technician student wants to check whether two prescription drugs interact. Which source is most authoritative?
options: A health forum where patients describe side effects
The prescribing information provided with each drug
A news article on the most prescribed drugs of the year
A friend who has taken both medicines without a problem
C.why: Official prescribing information lists known drug interactions and is written for health professionals, making it the most authoritative choice.

whyNot.0: Patient forum posts are anecdotes, not verified interaction data.
whyNot.2: A list of popular drugs does not address this pair's interactions.
whyNot.3: One person's experience is an anecdote and cannot rule out an interaction.

reteach.title: Think of asking for directions
reteach.question: You are lost in a new city. You could ask a tourist, a street vendor who has worked that corner for 20 years, or check an old paper map. Who do you trust, and does it depend on what you are asking?

blocks.body: For the nearest coffee shop, the street vendor is perfect: local, current, specific. For the train schedule, the station's posted timetable beats the vendor. For the history of the old church, a guidebook or the church's own records are better than either. The tourist is friendly but not an authority, and the old paper map may show streets that have changed. The best source depends on the question.

blocks.text: The friendliest or loudest helper (the most popular post) is not always the most reliable. Ask who actually knows, and whether their information is current.

explain.body: Name the need first: a firsthand view (primary), an explanation (secondary), a quick fact or definition (tertiary) or official current information (agency, label, schedule).

test.q: A student needs the average yearly rainfall for several US cities for a quick comparison. Which source fits best?
options: An almanac
A thesaurus
A glossary
A bibliography
test.why: An almanac compiles yearly facts and statistics, such as rainfall by city, for quick reference.

whyNot.1: A thesaurus lists synonyms, not statistics.
whyNot.2: A glossary defines key terms; it does not compile data.
whyNot.3: A bibliography lists the sources an author used, not facts about cities.

explain.body: Prefer the source that actually holds the information: the manufacturer's label for a dose, the transit authority for schedules, a government health agency for public health guidance, the school for its own requirements.

test.q: Which source is most authoritative for the hours of a county's public health clinic?
options: A map app's listing edited by users
A review site where patients rate clinics
The county health department's website
A neighbor who visited the clinic in spring
test.why: The county health department runs the clinic, so its website is the official source for the clinic's hours.

whyNot.0: User-edited listings may be inaccurate or outdated.
whyNot.1: Review sites focus on opinions, and their hours may not be maintained.
whyNot.3: A neighbor's visit months ago is secondhand and may be out of date.

explain.body: Some information changes often (schedules, doses, health guidance, admission rules), so an old source can be wrong even if it was expert. Other information changes rarely (a word's pronunciation, a historical date).

test.q: For which research question would the publication date of a source matter MOST?
options: When the first US nursing school opened
How the word 'triage' is pronounced
What the current guidance is for flu shots
Who wrote a famous 19th-century nursing book
test.why: Health guidance such as flu shot recommendations is updated over time, so an older source could be out of date.

whyNot.0: A historical date does not change, so an older reliable source still works.
whyNot.1: Pronunciation of a word rarely changes.
whyNot.3: The author of a historical book does not change over time.

explain.body: When two sources are both reliable and current, choose the one that matches your exact case: your county, your drug, this year, this program. A national or general source is less useful for a local question.

test.q: A clinic manager wants to know how many patients in her own city used the emergency room last month. All four sources below are official and current. Which is most useful?
options: A state report on ER use across all its counties
A national report on ER visits by age group
A federal report on hospital staffing trends
The city hospital council's monthly ER report
test.why: The city hospital council's monthly report matches her exact place and time period, making it the most specific choice.

whyNot.0: A statewide report is broader than her city and may not separate it out.
whyNot.1: A national report is far too general for one city.
whyNot.2: A staffing report does not count ER patients at all.
